t.2.97.1: Rāma, having comforted that brother of his who was devoted to his elders, then began, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, to question him.
t.2.97.2: What is this? I would like to hear it told by you: for what reason have you come to this land wearing bark garments, matted locks and a deerskin?
t.2.97.3: You ought to tell me all of that: for what reason you have left the kingdom and entered this region, wearing a black antelope skin and matted locks.
t.2.97.4: Thus addressed by the great-souled Kākutstha, the son of Kekayī, once more holding on firmly, spoke these words with his palms joined in reverence.
t.2.97.5: Having abandoned the noble one and done a most difficult deed, our mighty-armed father has gone to heaven, tormented by grief for his son.
t.2.97.6: Urged on by a woman, by Kaikeyī my mother, O scorcher of foes, he committed this exceedingly great sin, which robs him of his own fame.
t.2.97.7: My mother, widowed and wasted by grief, will not obtain the fruit of the kingdom; she will fall into a most terrible hell.
t.2.97.8: You should show favor to me, who have become your servant, and have yourself consecrated with the kingship this very day, as Maghavan was.
t.2.97.9: All these subjects, and the widowed mothers who have come into your presence: you ought to show them your grace.
t.2.97.11: May the whole earth, with you as her lord, be no longer a widow, just as an autumn night is with the spotless moon.
t.2.97.10: Then, O bestower of honour, righteously take up the kingdom that is rightly yours by order of succession and fitting for you, and make your friends fulfilled in their desires.
t.2.97.12: Entreated by me with bowed head, together with these ministers, you ought to show favor to your brother, your disciple, your servant.
t.2.97.13: O tiger among men, I cannot bring myself to disregard this whole circle of counsellors, long-standing, inherited from my father, and held in honour.
t.2.97.14: Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Bharata, son of Kekayī, his eyes filled with tears, once again clasped Rāma's feet with his head.
t.2.97.15: Rāma embraced his brother Bharata, who was sighing again and again like an elephant in rut, and spoke these words to him.
t.2.97.16: How could a man like you, nobly born, endowed with goodness, full of splendor and steadfast in his vows, commit a sin for the sake of a kingdom?
t.2.97.17: I see no fault in you, not even the slightest, O slayer of foes. Nor should you, out of childish folly, reproach your mother.
t.2.97.18: O knower of dharma, as great as the reverence owed to a father honoured by the world, so great, O best of the upholders of dharma, is the reverence owed to a mother as well.
t.2.97.20: You are to obtain the kingship in Ayodhyā, honored by the world, while I am to dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, clad in garments of bark.
t.2.97.19: O Rāghava, I have been told "Go to the forest" by these two, my mother and father, whose nature is devoted to dharma. How can I do anything else?
t.2.97.21: Having thus made the division in the presence of the people, and having given his instructions, the great king Daśaratha, of great splendor, went to heaven.
t.2.97.22: And that righteous-souled king, the teacher of the world, is your authority. You ought to enjoy, according to your share, what has been given to you by your father.
t.2.97.23: Having taken refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest for fourteen years, O gentle one, I shall enjoy the portion given to me by my great-souled father.
t.2.97.24: What my great-souled father, honored in the world of men and equal to the lord of the gods, told me, that alone I consider truly beneficial to myself, and not the imperishable state of lordship over all the worlds.
